questions.q: Per this lesson, what does the manifest's `eventHandlers` section actually do?
options: Maps each contract event signature to the name of the handler function that should process it
Declares which GraphQL entities are immutable
Lists the RPC providers a subgraph is allowed to use
Defines the GraphQL query URL the subgraph will be served from
questions.explain: The real manifest screenshot in this lesson shows exactly this: each event paired with a handler name, like Transfer paired with handleTransfer.

questions.q: What language does mapping.ts actually compile to, per this lesson?
options: WebAssembly, via AssemblyScript — a stricter subset of TypeScript
Plain JavaScript run directly in Node.js
Solidity bytecode deployed on-chain
Python, via a Graph-maintained transpiler
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that mapping.ts looks like TypeScript but compiles to WebAssembly through AssemblyScript, with no dynamic typing or arbitrary npm packages.

questions.q: In this lesson's immutable-entity example, what are the two calls that make up the entity's entire lifecycle?
options: Constructing it with `new Transfer(id)` and then calling `.save()`
Calling `.load()` then `.delete()`
Calling `.fetch()` then `.cache()`
Calling `.mutate()` then `.commit()`
questions.explain: For an immutable entity like Transfer, the lesson shows building it with `new Transfer(id)`, filling fields from event.params, then `.save()` — nothing more.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say `Account.load()` returning null is the normal case, not an error?
options: Because the first-ever transfer to an address means no Account entity exists yet, so the handler must create one before mutating it
Because Account.load() always returns null on AssemblyScript's WebAssembly runtime
Because mutable entities cannot be loaded, only created fresh every time
Because null indicates the subgraph has failed to sync
questions.explain: The load-or-create pattern exists exactly because an address's first-ever transfer has no prior Account entity — null means "create it," not "something broke."

questions.q: Why must a mapping handler be pure and deterministic, according to this lesson?
options: Every indexer syncing the same subgraph must compute the exact same entities from the exact same events, or different indexers would disagree about the result
AssemblyScript's compiler rejects any function that isn't marked pure
Determinism is only required for entities marked immutable, not mutable ones
It isn't actually required — the lesson says handlers may safely call external APIs
questions.explain: The lesson explains this directly: no fetch(), no clock, no randomness, because indexers across the network must independently compute identical results from identical events.
